questions.stem: What defines a limiting factor?

options.text: Something in short supply that restricts a life process
options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.
Consumption alone does not limit the rate.

options.text: The factor present in greatest amount
options.explanation: Abundance does not restrict anything.
Only the scarce one limits at a given moment.

questions.stem: Why is water not usually a limiting factor for photosynthesis?

options.explanation: Shortage is rare relative to demand.

options.text: The amount photosynthesis needs is tiny compared with what the plant loses by transpiration
options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.

options.text: Water is not involved in photosynthesis
options.explanation: Water is a raw material of the reaction.
Storage is finite; the demand is just small.

questions.stem: Why does the rate fall at high temperatures?

options.text: Carbon dioxide dissolves out of the leaf
options.explanation: The collapse is driven by denaturation.

options.text: Chlorophyll reflects more light when hot
options.explanation: Pigment optics are unchanged.

options.text: The enzymes controlling photosynthesis denature, so their active sites no longer fit substrates
options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.

options.text: Water evaporates from the leaf completely
options.explanation: Loss happens, but the stated cause is enzyme shape.

questions.stem: What happens to collision frequency as temperature rises within the workable range?

options.text: Collisions stop entirely at high temperature
options.explanation: They continue until denaturation intervenes.

options.text: Particles lose energy as it warms
options.explanation: Kinetic energy rises with temperature.
It clearly is not.

options.text: Particles gain kinetic energy, so successful collisions become more frequent
options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.

questions.stem: Which additional quantity can cap the rate besides the three main factors?

options.text: The number of chloroplasts, or the chlorophyll they contain
options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.
Sand is not the stated influence.
Height is not cited as a rate factor.
The corpus cites chloroplasts and chlorophyll.

questions.stem: Name the three main limiting factors of photosynthesis.
questions.modelAnswer: Temperature, light intensity and carbon dioxide concentration.

questions.stem: State what denaturation means for an enzyme's active site.
questions.modelAnswer: The active site's shape shifts and no longer complements its substrate.

questions.stem: Explain why the temperature graph for photosynthesis rises and then falls.
questions.modelAnswer: Because warming first speeds the collisions between reactants and enzymes, lifting the rate, but beyond the optimum the enzymes denature, their active sites lose their fit, and the rate falls away instead of continuing to climb.

questions.stem: A greenhouse runs at its optimal temperature all day. State what becomes the limiting factor and why.
questions.modelAnswer: With temperature no longer restricting, the scarcest remaining resource — usually carbon dioxide concentration or light intensity — becomes the limiting factor, since the rate can only rise as far as that resource allows.

questions.stem: What does increasing light intensity supply to the plant?

options.explanation: Chloroplast count is fixed in the tissue.

options.text: More energy for carrying out photosynthesis
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.
Carbon dioxide and water are the raw materials.
Light does not create enzymes.

questions.stem: Why does the light-intensity curve eventually flatten?

options.text: Light damages the leaf beyond a point
options.explanation: Damage is not the stated mechanism.
Rates plateau, they do not diverge.

options.text: Some other factor runs short and becomes the limiting one
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.

options.text: The plant runs out of chlorophyll entirely
options.explanation: Chlorophyll persists; the plateau has another cause.

questions.stem: Why does added carbon dioxide speed photosynthesis?

options.explanation: Light energy comes from illumination.
Gas concentration and temperature are separate.
Denaturation slows reactions; CO2 speeds this one.

options.text: Carbon dioxide is a raw material, so more of it lets the reaction proceed faster
options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.

questions.stem: On the carbon dioxide graph, which factors may set the plateau?

options.text: Light intensity or temperature, whichever is scarcest
options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.
The plotted variable cannot limit its own curve's rise.
Chlorophyll matters but is not the stated plateau-setter here.
Water is rarely limiting for photosynthesis.

questions.stem: A plant in bright light and warm air shows a flat rate despite extra light. What is limiting?

options.explanation: The corpus treats water shortage as rare.

options.text: Carbon dioxide concentration, the next scarcest resource
options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.
The stem says the air is warm.
Increasing the plotted factor does not cap the curve.

questions.stem: State the shape shared by the light and carbon dioxide rate curves.
questions.modelAnswer: Each rises at first and then plateaus once another factor becomes limiting.

questions.stem: Name the raw material whose concentration is plotted against rate.
questions.modelAnswer: Carbon dioxide, one of the raw materials of photosynthesis.

questions.stem: Explain why the plateau position differs between two plants with different chlorophyll amounts.
questions.modelAnswer: Because a plant with fewer chloroplasts or less chlorophyll captures light energy less effectively, so its rate caps lower and earlier; the plateau it reaches sits beneath the one a chlorophyll-rich plant attains under the same conditions.

questions.stem: A grower wants faster photosynthesis in winter. Using the two curves, decide the first variable to raise.
questions.modelAnswer: In winter, light intensity is typically the scarcest resource, so raising illumination is the first lever; once the light curve plateaus, carbon dioxide enrichment becomes the next step, and temperature should already be controlled.

questions.stem: What does chlorophyll do in photosynthesis?

options.text: It fixes carbon dioxide into glucose
options.explanation: Chlorophyll captures energy, not carbon.
Storage happens elsewhere in the plant.

options.text: It absorbs the light energy that the process runs on
options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.

options.text: It splits water into oxygen directly
options.explanation: Absorption of light is the stated role.

questions.stem: Where is chlorophyll housed?

options.explanation: The pigment sits in organelles, not free in sap.
The wall is outside the membrane.
The vacuole stores sap, not pigment.

options.text: Inside chloroplasts in the leaf's cells
options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.

questions.stem: How does raising chloroplast number affect the rate?

options.text: More chloroplasts capture more light energy, so the rate rises
options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.

options.text: The rate falls as organelles crowd the cell
options.explanation: Crowding is not the stated effect.

options.text: The rate is unaffected by chloroplast count
options.explanation: The corpus states it matters.
Unrelated mechanisms.

questions.stem: Which leaf layer exploits chloroplast packing most visibly?

options.explanation: It transports substances, not light capture.

options.text: The palisade mesophyll, with tightly packed chloroplast-rich cells
options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.
The cuticle is a protective layer without chloroplasts.
It hosts guard cells and stomata.

questions.stem: Why does pigment amount not replace the environmental factors?

options.explanation: Denaturation applies to enzymes.
They manufacture, not consume.

options.text: Because without sufficient light, warmth and carbon dioxide, even abundant chlorophyll cannot raise the rate
options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.
It works whenever light is absorbed.

questions.stem: State the function of chlorophyll in one sentence.
questions.modelAnswer: Chlorophyll is the green pigment that absorbs light energy for photosynthesis.

questions.stem: Name the organelle containing chlorophyll.
Explain why more chloroplasts raise the rate only up to a point.
questions.modelAnswer: Because extra pigment raises the capture of light energy, but once another resource — carbon dioxide or temperature — becomes limiting, the reaction cannot speed further no matter how much light is absorbed.

questions.stem: Two identical seedlings differ only in chlorophyll amount. Predict which photosynthesises faster in dim light and justify.
questions.modelAnswer: The chlorophyll-rich seedling, because in dim light capture of the scarce photons is the bottleneck and extra pigment harvests more of the limited energy, lifting its rate above the pale seedling's.
